Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg., cor EDSA Mapagmahal Street, Diliman, Quezon City LEGAL SERVICE DILG OPINION NO. 6) S. 2010 24 May 2010 PUNONG BARANGAY BENJAMIN P. RIVERA Barangay Siena, Quezon City Dear PB Rivera: This has reference to your earlier letter addressed to DILG-Quezon City Director Maria Lourdes L. Agustin asking that level's legal opinion relative to the conduct of your sangguniang barangay's regular session and the claim for honoraria of several sangguniang barangay members thereat. Thereafter, City Director Agustin indorsed your letter as well as the rejoinder of the majority of the sangguniang Barangay members to this level for appropriate action and summarized the issues as follows: "1) Whether or not halfofthe honorarium of the majority of the sangguniang barangay members who were unable to attend their regular council meeting (which was, nevertheless, adjourned due to lack of quorum) may be legally withheld by the punong barangay? Reading from the position of the concerned sangguniang barangay members, it is their contention that they should be paid of their honorarium considering that their regular council session was adjourned due to lack of quorum. e) Whether or not the council session called and conducted by majority of the sangguniang members and presided by SK Chairman Lawrence Ortiz last 25 January 2010 may be considered regular session in lieu of their 16 January 2010 regular session which was adjourned due to lack of quorum? S) Whether or not Kagawad Emma Lourdes C. De Jesus and Kagawad Ernesto G. Gomez, who were preventively suspended by the Quezon City Council on 06 January '2010, are entitled to half of their honorarium due to the Stay Order by the Office of the President dated 11 January 2010, and was served by this ofiice on 18 January 201 OP It is the contention PB Benjamin P. Rivera that since Kagawad Emma Lordes C. De Jesus and Kagawad Ernesto G. Gomez were unable to attend their two (e) regular council sessions for the month of January 2010, their honorarium should be withheld until final resolution of their suspension. ' We shall answer your first and second queries in one discussion since they pertain to one (1) subject matter.

-2- In reply thereto, please be informed that under DBM Loca/ Budget Circular No. 63, in relation to Section 393 of the Local Government Code of 1991, Sangguniang Barangay Members are paid in the form of honorarium. The Government Accounting and Auditing Manual (GAAM) defines honorarium as that remuneration given to a public official for services actually rendered. In the case of Santiago vs. COA (GR No. 92284, 12 July 1991) "An honorarium is defined as something given not as a matter of obligation but in appreciation for services rendered a voluntary donation in consideration of services which admit of no compensation in money: With this, it has been our considered view that in measuring the services actually rendered by an elective barangay official, the basic consideration shall be his attendance in regular and special sessions. A regular session is that which has been earlier fixed as to day, time and place, through a Resolution passed by the sanggunian concerned on the first day of the session immediately following the election of its members [Section 52 (a), Loca/ Government Code of 1991]. Sangguniang barangays are mandated to conduct two (2) regular sessions a month (Ibid.). Since the day, time and place of the regular session was already fixed via a Resolution, we are of the view that a written notice for the holding of such regular session is no longer required. A special session, on the other hand, is that which may be called by the local chief executive or by a majority of the members of the sanggunian when public interest so demands [Section 52 (d), Loca/ Government Code of 1991]. In calling such special sessions, it is required that a written notice to the members shall be served personally at the member's usual place of residence at least twenty-four (24) hours before the special session is held (Ibid.). It bears to stress that-any session held on a day other than the scheduled date of regular session is properly considered a special session so that it should comply with the requirements set forth under Section 52 (d) of the Code. Should an elective barangay official be absent in a session of the sangguniang barangay for reasons other than the performance of his public duty outside of the office, such as attending to the problems of the constituents, he may suffer a proportionate reduction of his honoraria. In the case at hand, according to you, several members of the sangguniang barangay did not attend your 16 January 2010 regular session since the notice for the said session was only given to them on 15 January 2010 and that they had already emergency appointments set on that session day. With only you and two (2) sangguniang barangay members present, the aforesaid 16 January 2010 regular session was adjourned for lack of quorum. As contended by the majority of your sangguniang barangay members in their rejoinder, they should be given their honoraria corresponding to your 16 January 2010 regular session since the same was after all adjourned due to lack of quorum. Applying the rule as we enunciated above, written notices for the conduct of a sanggunian's regular session are no longer required since the date, time and place of the regular session was already previously fixed via a Resolution. The sangguniang barangay members cannot therefore use good faith (e.g. short

-3- notice) as a defense for not attending the sangguniang barangay's regular session. Corollary thereto, since several sangguniang barangay members did not attend your 16 January 2010 regular session due to their emergency appointments, we find the proportionate reduction of their respective honoraria to be just proper if such emergency appointments are not connected with the performance of their public duty. The foregoing rule on the proportionate reduction of honoraria is also true even if the regular session was nevertheless adjourned due to lack of quorum. May we respectfully stress that on 16 January 2010, there was still a regular session that took place but the same was only adjourned due to lack of quorum. This holding of a regular session, though momentarily, was corroborated in your letter when you said that "(T)he Chairman therefore opened the Session at 2:40PM with on/y Kagawads Carolina Cruz and Primitivo Perez, Jr. present. The Secretary informed the Chairman that there are on/y three (3) members in the quorum including the Chairman. The Chairman therefore declared it a non- quorum and adjourned the Session at 2:45PM. "There was nothing to adjourn if there was no regular session that took place in the first place. Furthermore, a quorum is defined under Section 53 of the Local Government Code of 1991 as "(A) majority ofa// the members of the sanggunian who have been elected and qualified xxx. " It is settled that the existence of a quorum is necessary in order for the sanggunian to transact official business. May it be remembered that the existence or non-existence of a quorum is usually determined after a roll call of the members, which is usually made before every session starts. This attendance to session is already sufficient to entitle a sangguniang barangay member to his honoraria. To hold that even sangguniang barangay members who did not attend the 16 January 2010 regular session are entitled to honoraria corresponding to this particular regular session would run counter to the rule that honorarium is given only as a remuneration to a public official for services he actually rendered. Besides, it would be unfair to those sangguniang barangay members who were present and willing to participate in that 16 January 2010 regular session if even those who were absent due to personal reasons are equally given their honoraria. With regard to your third query, may we invite your attention to Sections 68 and 64 of the Local Government Code of 1991, to wit: "SECTION 68. Execution Pending Appeal.—An appeal shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory. The respondent shall be considered as having been placed under preventive suspension during the pendency of an appeal in the event he wins such appeal. In the event the appeal results in an exoneration, he shall be paid his salary and such other emoluments during the pendency of the appeal. "SECTION 64. Salary of Respondent Pending Suspension.—The respondent official preventively suspended from office shall receive no salary or compensation during such suspension; but, upon subsequent exoneration and reinstatement, he shall be paid full salary or compensation

-4- including such emoluments accruing during such suspension." Based on the aforequoted Section 68 of the Code, the respondent local elective official shall be considered as having placed under preventive suspension during the pendency of his appeal. Relative thereto, under Section 64 of the Code, the respondent local elective official preventively suspended from office shall receive no salary or compensation during such suspension and it is only upon his exoneration and reinstatement that he shall be paid his full salary or compensation, including such emoluments accruing during such suspension. In the case at hand, while Sangguniang Barangay Members Emma Lourdes C. De Jesus and Ernesto G. Gomez were meted the penalty of suspension (not preventive suspension as indicated by City Director Agustin in her letter), they successfully obtained a Stay Order from the Office of the It was by virtue of the said Stay Order from the Office of the President. President that the implementation of their penalty of suspension was, in the meantime, held in abeyance so that Sangguniang Barangay Members De Jesus and Gomez were directed to re-assume their duties as sangguniang barangay members pending their appeal. Let it be noted that the non-implementation of the suspension against Sangguniang Barangay Members De Jesus and Gomez does not automatically entitle them too of their respective honoraria. They are still required to attend their sangguniang barangay's regular and special sessions. This is only proper since Sangguniang Barangay Members are paid in the form of honorarium, which is defined as that remuneration given to a public official for services actually rendered. As we already explained above, in measuring the services actually rendered by an elective barangay official, the basic consideration shall be his attendance in regular and special sessions. Thus, a sangguniang barangay member may suffer a proportionate reduction of his honoraria for his failure to attend a session for reasons other than the performance of his public duty outside of the office, such as attending to the problems of the constituents. We hope this finally settles your concern. Very truly yours, BY AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: cc: Ls/17 A USEC. EDUARDO R. SOLIMAN, JR. Undersecretary for Special Constituency Relations This Department DIR. MARIA LOURDES L. AGUSTIN City Director DILG, Quezon City . DOQ EIV . JESU Director III
